entries.name: Rolled cylinder
entries.description: A rolled cylinder is a plain sheet rolled into a round shell and seamed along its length. It is the most common piece in a fabrication shop: tank and silo shells, chimney and flue sections, round duct, pipe made from plate, guards and hoppers all start as one. The flat is a rectangle whose length is the shell's girth, measured at the right point through the sheet's thickness so that the rolled shell comes out at the diameter asked for. Getting that girth right is what makes the seam close without a gap or an overlap.

sizes.label: 1000 mm diameter, 800 mm high, 6 mm plate
630 mm duct diameter, 1000 mm long, 1 mm sheet

entries.name: Cone and frustum
entries.description: A cone or frustum joins two round sections of different size on one centre line: a concentric reducer in round duct or pipe work, the bottom of a hopper or silo, a nozzle, a funnel or a chimney cap. The flat is a ring sector, a part of the space between two circles, rolled until its two straight edges meet. Its two arc radii and the angle of the sector are what a shop marks out; they are listed with each size here, so the flat can also be checked by hand before it is cut.

entries.name: Oblique and eccentric cone
entries.description: An oblique or eccentric cone joins two round sections whose centres are not in line: an eccentric reducer that keeps the bottom of a pipe or duct level, an offset hopper outlet, or a reducer that has to clear a beam. The flat is no longer a simple ring sector, since every line from the small end to the large end has its own length. Each size here gives the flat's overall size and a cut file to the exact outline, ready to roll and seam.

sizes.label: 1000 mm to 500 mm, offset 200 mm, 6 mm plate

entries.name: Multi-course shell
entries.description: A tall shell, a silo, a stack or a tank, is made of courses: rings of plate as wide as the sheet, stacked and welded one on another. Where the shell narrows, the courses are cone frustums. This entry gives each course's flat as its own cut file, so that every plate in the shell can be cut from stock sheet and rolled to the right diameter at both of its edges, with the courses meeting where they should.

entries.name: Square-to-round
entries.description: A square-to-round joins a square or rectangular opening to a round one: the connection from a rectangular duct to a round duct or fan, a hopper outlet on a round chute, or a chimney base. It is one of the most searched-for flat patterns in sheet metal work. The flat is made of flat triangles at the corners and curved cones between them, folded along lines marked on the flat. Each size here gives the flat in one piece with its fold lines.

entries.name: Round-to-round transition
entries.description: A round-to-round transition joins two round sections that are offset, tilted or both: an offset reducer that has to step across, the joint between a round duct and a sloping roof or wall, or a hopper that changes direction as it narrows. Where the ends are on one centre line it is a plain cone; here they need not be. Each size gives the flat in one piece, ready to roll and seam.

entries.name: Rectangle-to-rectangle and hopper
entries.description: A rectangle-to-rectangle piece joins two rectangular openings: a hopper or bin outlet, a pyramid hood, a rectangular reducer or a machine guard. The sides are flat panels folded at the corners on a press brake, so the flat carries a fold line at each corner and the bend allowance comes from the shop's own table of material, thickness and K-factor. Each size here gives the flat with its fold lines, ready to cut and fold.

entries.name: Transition between any two sections
entries.description: A transition joins any two sections: a rectangle, a circle, an oval, an obround or any straight-sided outline at each end, offset, turned or tilted as the job needs. It covers the awkward connections no catalogue piece fits, between plant of different makes, through a tight ceiling space or onto an odd-shaped outlet. Each size here gives the flat with its fold lines in one piece.

entries.name: Segmented (lobster-back) elbow
entries.description: A segmented or lobster-back elbow turns a round pipe or duct through an angle in short straight pieces, each cut at a slant at both ends. It is how large pipe, round duct, chimney flues and exhaust stacks are bent where no pressed bend is made. Each piece is a rolled cylinder whose flat has curved ends; this entry gives every piece's flat as its own cut file, the end pieces half the length of the middle ones.

sizes.label: 300 mm diameter, 90 degrees in 4 pieces, 3 mm plate

entries.name: Reducing segmented elbow
entries.description: A reducing segmented elbow turns and narrows at once: each piece is a short cone cut at a slant at both ends, so that the bend goes from a large diameter to a smaller one. It is used on cyclone inlets, fan outlets, dust extraction and chutes where there is no room for a bend and a reducer one after the other. This entry gives every piece's flat as its own cut file.

sizes.label: 400 mm to 250 mm, 90 degrees in 4 pieces, 3 mm plate

entries.name: Tee
entries.description: A tee is a round branch meeting a round main at right angles, set on the main or set into it. The branch's end is the saddle, or fishmouth, cut that fits the main, and the main carries the hole the branch meets. Pipe fitters, duct makers and fabricators lay it out on every job. Each size here gives the main's flat with its hole and the branch's flat with its shaped end, as cut files.

entries.name: Y-piece (breeches)
entries.description: A breeches or Y-piece splits one round main into two or more branches, or joins them into one: dust extraction and pneumatic conveying, chutes, exhausts and hot-air ducts. The main and each leg meet along shared cut edges, so every piece's end is shaped to fit the others. This entry gives the main's and each leg's flats as their own cut files, the legs to the angles given.
